cards.explanation: The answer is his anxious thoughts. Zophar says it himself: "So my anxious thoughts compel me to answer, because of the turmoil within me." (Job 20:2) So he isn't claiming a message from above. He's saying the turmoil inside him is doing the pushing. I think we've all hit send while our stomach was still doing flips.

The answer is True. Zophar says it right out: "I have heard a rebuke that insults me, and my understanding prompts a reply." (Job 20:3) He says the rebuke insults him, and then his understanding prompts a reply. I think that's why he's answering with both hands on the wheel.

The answer is since man was placed on the earth. Zophar asks, "Do you not know that from antiquity, since man was placed on the earth…" (Job 20:4). He's reaching back to the very start of people on earth. That's about as far back as a claim can go.

The answer is brief. Zophar says "…the triumph of the wicked has been brief and the joy of the godless momentary?" (Job 20:5) Brief and momentary, he says, and he says it's been that way the whole time. That's the point he's about to spend a whole speech on.
The answer is perish. Zophar says "…he will perish forever…" (Job 20:7). The head can touch the clouds, and he still says the man perishes. That's a long fall, and Zophar doesn't soften it.

The answer is True. Zophar says "those who had seen him will ask, ‘Where is he?’" (Job 20:7) The people who used to see him are the ones who ask it. Once you're gone, folks can only ask where you went.
The answer is False. Zophar says, "The eye that saw him will see him no more…" (Job 20:9). No someday in there. He says the eye won't see him again.

The answer is that the sons seek the favor of the poor. Here's what Zophar says: "His sons will seek the favor of the poor, for his own hands must return his wealth." (Job 20:10) So the sons are the ones seeking the favor of the poor. Zophar doesn't say how that goes.

The answer is lying with him in the dust. Here's the line: "The youthful vigor that fills his bones will lie down with him in the dust." (Job 20:11) All that energy ends up lying down in the dust right along with him. I spent a long stretch in the dark of a junk drawer, friends, and I'm glad I got dusted off.

The answer is that his food sours into cobra venom. Zophar says, "…yet in his stomach his food sours into the venom of cobras within him." (Job 20:14) It tasted sweet going in, and it turns the other way inside. That's a stomachache nobody wants.

The word is wealth. Zophar says, "He swallows wealth but vomits it out; God will force it from his stomach." (Job 20:15) The wealth goes down and comes back up. And Zophar says it's God who forces it out.
The answer is False. Zophar says, "He will not enjoy the streams, the rivers flowing with honey and cream." (Job 20:17) Rivers of honey and cream, and he doesn't get to enjoy them. Rough.

The reason is that he oppressed and forsook the poor. Zophar says, "For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor…" (Job 20:19). He says the man oppressed the poor and left them. I'll say it once, friends, this is the heavy part of the speech.

The answer is True. Zophar says, "he has seized houses he did not build." (Job 20:19) Houses somebody else built, and the man grabbed them. Zophar lists it right alongside oppressing and forsaking the poor.

The answer is that it is never satisfied. Zophar says, "Because his appetite is never satisfied, he cannot escape with his treasure." (Job 20:20) Never satisfied is a tough way to live. It's like I always say about the cookie jar: there's no such thing as the last one.

The answer is False. Zophar says, "In the midst of his plenty, he will be distressed; the full force of misery will come upon him." (Job 20:22) So he has plenty, and he still gets distress. No peace in that sentence.

The answer is True. Zophar says, "When he has filled his stomach, God will vent His fury upon him, raining it down on him as he eats." (Job 20:23) It comes right while he's eating. This is Zophar's claim about God, friends, and the story isn't done with it.

The answer is that a bronze-tipped arrow pierces him. Zophar says, "Though he flees from an iron weapon, a bronze-tipped arrow will pierce him." (Job 20:24) He runs from one weapon and the next one finds him. It's a grim picture.

The answer is what is left in his tent. Zophar says, "A fire unfanned will consume him and devour what is left in his tent." (Job 20:26) The fire takes both the man and what's left in his tent. It's one more picture of everything going.
The word is expose. Zophar says, "The heavens will expose his iniquity, and the earth will rise up against him." (Job 20:27) The sky shows his sin out in the open. Nowhere left to hide.

The answer is the wicked man's portion from God. Zophar closes with, "This is the wicked man’s portion from God, the inheritance God has appointed him." (Job 20:29) That's how he sums up the whole speech. It's what Zophar says, friends, and the conversation keeps going.
